  • A gateway in front of providers. Direct provider SDK calls buried in business logic are the thing I most regret shipping, because routing, retries, fallback, and key management end up reimplemented in every feature.
  • A rollback story. Prompts are versioned, models are pinned, and any release reverts in minutes.

Anything missing one of these is a prototype that happens to be running in production.

Why the bottleneck moved from training to evaluation

Two years ago the conversation was model selection and fine-tuning. It has flipped, for three reasons I watched play out. Frontier APIs got cheap enough that using a frontier-quality model for routine traffic is economical, and self-hosting a small open model is cheaper but only narrowly. Open models closed the quality gap on narrow tasks when fine-tuned. And the hard problems moved up the stack: hallucinations, prompt injection, tool failures, drift on new user populations, and audit trails are not solved by scaling parameters, they are observability and evaluation problems.

So building for production in 2026 is mostly the discipline of running a tight eval and observability loop while picking sensible defaults for everything else.

Step 1: define the eval gate, not the model

Before I open a provider dashboard, I write two things down. The user-visible promise, meaning what the feature does and what the worst-case failure looks like for a user. And the acceptance criteria, meaning what scores on what dataset would let me ship.

Concretely that is a golden set of 100 to 500 examples covering the head and the long tail of expected inputs, plus a target on a defined metric. For a support assistant, that might be groundedness above 0.85, context adherence above 0.9, and a custom policy-compliance judge above 0.95. That is the eval gate, and every later step is a decision about whether I cleared it. Writing the gate before the model is the single habit that has saved me the most rework.

Step 2: get the data right before you pick a model

Even with frontier models, data is where most production projects fail, and three traps catch me most.

  • Coverage gaps. The golden set over-represents easy cases, so I sample new examples from the production trace log weekly.
  • Ground-truth ambiguity. Two annotators disagree on the correct answer, and until that is resolved the eval gate is measuring noise, not quality.
  • Leakage. Golden-set examples sneak into the few-shot prompt or the fine-tuning set, so hash and dedupe.

For retrieval apps the data step also includes a chunking and indexing strategy and a separate retrieval-quality eval, precision and recall at k plus a generative check like context adherence on the final answer.

Step 3: pick a base model, and a backup

There is no single right answer, and the defaults that work for most teams look like this.

Workload Primary Backup Complex reasoning, code, tool use A frontier reasoning model The other frontier model Long-context retrieval, multimodal A long-context frontier model A second frontier model High-volume classification, routing A small frontier model A self-hosted small open model Style or schema enforcement A fine-tuned small open model A frontier model with strict JSON schema Regulated, on-prem only A mid-size open model Another open model

The move is almost never to lock in one provider. Route through a gateway, evaluate both candidates on your own task, and keep the cheaper one as primary with the pricier one as fallback for low-confidence outputs.

Step 4: train, fine-tune, or skip

For most knowledge-grounded tasks, retrieval plus a frontier model beats a fine-tuned smaller model on cost, freshness, and latency. I fine-tune only when one of these is true: I need strict JSON-only or domain-vocabulary output, I need sub-200ms latency and can host a small model, I operate in a regulated domain where the weights must stay on my hardware, or I have a style that prompting cannot enforce cheaply. Whatever I choose, I evaluate the tuned model against the same golden set and the same evaluators I would use on a frontier baseline, because a fine-tune that scores worse than the baseline plus a better prompt is a sunk cost.

Step 5: deploy behind a gateway

Direct completion calls inside application code are the pattern I have torn out of the most codebases. In 2026 the route is: app to gateway to provider to response to eval to trace and back. The gateway owns key management across providers, routing rules like a cheap model for short prompts and a frontier model for long ones, retries and fallback and circuit breakers when a provider degrades, budget caps per route and team and environment, and a single point to inject guardrails and PII scrubbing.

The point is not which gateway. The point is that something owns the routing concern instead of every feature reimplementing it. Behind the gateway, every response flows through an OpenTelemetry tracing layer so any request can be replayed, with the user ID, the prompt version, and the response all on the span.

Step 6: evaluate production traffic continuously

The eval gate stops bad changes from shipping. Continuous evaluation catches what the gate could not predict: distribution shift, new prompt-injection patterns, tool failures, and silent quality drops. In practice I run evaluators on a sample of live traces, 1 to 5 percent for high-volume products and everything for low-volume high-stakes ones. Then I alert on rolling p95 score drops, not averages, because a 10 percent drop in the worst decile of responses matters more than a 2 percent move in the mean, and the mean is exactly where a real regression hides.

Step 7: monitor, scale, and roll back

By this point the work is closer to SRE than to ML research, and five things stay on the dashboard. Latency at p50, p95, and p99 per route and provider, because frontier APIs have multi-second tail latencies that surprise teams used to web SLOs. Token consumption and cost broken down by feature, since a surprise bill almost always traces to one feature looping. Quality scores over time by user segment. Tool-call success rate for agentic flows, which often causes more user-visible damage than a model-quality dip. And prompt-version pinning, so every request traces back to a known prompt, model pin, and gateway config. When something breaks, the rollback is a one-line gateway config change, not a code redeploy.

What actually separates the teams that ship

The teams that ship fastest are not the ones with the largest model. They are the ones that have a golden set and a defined eval gate, a gateway in front of every provider call, tracing on every request with continuous evaluators on sampled or high-stakes traffic, a one-line rollback for prompts and pins, and a weekly cadence of reading the lowest-scoring traces and feeding them back into the dataset. Everything else, including model selection and fine-tuning, is downstream of getting that loop right.

If you have taken an LLM feature from demo to production, I would like to know which of the seven bit you hardest. For me it is the eval gate, because every quarter I lose to a regression is a quarter I skipped writing the gate before the model.

posts.title: My PDF QA Bot Cited Page 47 of a 30-Page Contract. The Retriever Was the Bug.
posts.excerpt: A PDF QA chatbot is a retrieval problem, not a generation one. If the retriever surfaces the wrong chunk, a perfectly grounded answer is still wrong, and your generation scores…
posts.html:
A PDF QA chatbot is a retrieval problem, not a generation one. If the retriever surfaces the wrong chunk, a perfectly grounded answer is still wrong, and your generation scores will say it shipped fine.

The bot answered the easy questions and then confidently cited page 47 of a 30-page contract, returned the indemnity clause when asked about termination, and told a user the document said something it did not. The standup blamed the model. The trace said otherwise: the retriever surfaced the wrong chunk, and the model dutifully grounded its answer in it.

That is the failure most PDF QA tutorials skip. A query call returns something, and without retrieval and generation evals running on every change you cannot tell whether the something is right, or whether the regression you just shipped is the chunker, the retriever, the prompt, or the model. The lesson I keep relearning is that retrieval-level evaluation is the right primitive for a PDF QA bot, not generation evaluation alone. Generation rubrics reward grounding to whatever context the retriever fed in, so if the retriever surfaced the wrong chunk, a grounded answer is still wrong and the score says it passed. The retriever is the chatbot. The generator is how the retriever talks.

Here is the build with the eval baked in from step one.

Why most PDF QA bots ship broken

Three failure modes show up in production traces almost every time, and none of them surfaces if the eval only runs faithfulness on the final answer.

  • The wrong chunk gets retrieved. The user asks about Section 12, vector similarity surfaces Section 9, the generator grounds in Section 9, and groundedness passes.
  • The right chunks are retrieved and the model uses the wrong ones. The relevant chunks come back at ranks 1 and 4, the generator latches onto rank 1 and ignores rank 4, the answer omits a critical clause, and groundedness still passes.
  • A citation points at a chunk that does not contain the quoted span. The generator hallucinated the quote, structured output passed, schema validation passed, and the user is reading a fabricated citation that looks identical to a real one.

The first two are retrieval failures wearing a generation failure’s clothes. The third is a generation failure that needs a deterministic check, not a judge. The fix is to split the eval into a retrieval layer and a generation layer, gate both, and bridge both to production traces.

Step 1: parse with structure intact

PDFs lie about being simple text. A text PDF can carry multi-column layout, embedded tables, footnotes, sidebars, and figure captions, and a scanned PDF is an image that needs OCR. Most parsing bugs trace to lost structure: a parser that flattens a two-column page into interleaved nonsense, or drops a table into a wall of cells. Whichever parser you pick, its output has to preserve four fields on every element: page number, section heading, element type, and reading order. Those four fields are the difference between chunks the retriever can use and chunks that are noise. In regulated corpora, 20 percent of the documents showing up as image-only PDFs is common, and OCR quality sets the floor on your retrieval scores.

Step 2: chunk on a semantic boundary

Fixed-character chunking is the lazy default, and semantic chunking that respects document structure wins by 5 to 15 points on retrieval rubrics across the domains I have measured. The chunk is the unit of retrieval and attribution, so if the boundary cuts a clause in half, the citation will too. The chunker is a section walk: group elements by section, and start a new chunk when the section changes or the running size exceeds the embedding window. Three rules decide whether it earns its keep.

  • Keep tables and figure captions as their own chunks, and embed a table on its caption and header row rather than the full grid flattened into text.
  • Carry header context by prefixing each chunk with its section heading, so the embedding encodes “this is from the Liability section,” not just the body.
  • Cap the chunk at the embedding window minus headroom for that header prefix.

Evaluate the chunks before you embed them. The distribution of chunk sizes, the fraction that span a section boundary, and the fraction that include a table or caption are cheap to compute and predict the downstream retrieval scores tightly.

Step 3: hybrid retrieval, because pure vector loses

Pure vector search loses on identifier-heavy queries, and contract numbers, defined terms, clause IDs, statute references, drug names, and part numbers are exactly the queries that dominate enterprise PDF traffic. Pure keyword search loses the moment a user paraphrases. Hybrid retrieval, vector plus a keyword index fused with reciprocal rank fusion, wins both. Two things are non-negotiable on top of it. A per-tenant filter on every query, because a cross-tenant leak in a multi-customer deployment is a configuration failure, not a model one. And a query-rewrite step, which lifts recall on under-specified queries by a few points, though you should score both the rewrite and the final answer so you know which one helped.

Step 4: generate with citation enforcement

The generator is where hallucinations creep in even when retrieval did its job, and three controls compound. The output is a schema with a per-claim citation carrying the chunk ID and the quoted span, plus a confidence field. Each citation is validated deterministically before the answer leaves the bot: the chunk ID has to exist in the retrieved set, and the quoted span has to appear verbatim in that chunk. And there is a refusal path for when retrieval comes back empty or weak, with the prompt instructed to say so and drop its confidence. A failed citation validation does not ship. Retry once with a stricter prompt that names the failed citation, then fall back to a refusal rather than hand back a fabricated quote. Citation validity is the one check in the whole stack that does not need a judge, since a verbatim string match with a small fuzzy tolerance is enough, and the cheaper the check, the more often you can run it.

Step 5: split the eval suite by layer

Most teams write three rubrics on the final answer and call it eval, then regress for three quarters because they cannot tell whether the chunker, the retriever, the prompt, or the model moved. Split the rubrics by layer and the bisect becomes trivial.

  • Retrieval rubrics ask whether the retriever did its job: are the retrieved chunks relevant to the question, which retrieved chunks the answer actually used, and what fraction of the relevant content the answer used, which flags the generator ignoring good chunks.
  • Generation rubrics ask whether the generator did its job given the chunks it got: are the claims supported by the context, did the answer stay inside the context rather than importing outside knowledge, did it cover what the question asked, and are the asserted facts correct against ground truth.
  • The deterministic floor is citation validity: every cited span exists in the retrieved context, string match, no judge.

Three habits separate a real gate from theatre. Set per-rubric thresholds, and fail a change on a two-point drop from the trailing seven-day baseline while an absolute floor catches the catastrophic drops. Scope by route, so a change to the contract-bot prompt does not rerun the SOP-bot suite. And diff against a moving baseline, because the models drift and the baseline has to drift with them. For the dataset, 100 to 200 cases sampled from real user questions covers factual lookup, multi-hop reasoning, table extraction, refusal scenarios, ambiguous queries where the right move is to ask for clarification, and edge cases like footnotes, scanned pages, and captions. Grow it weekly by promoting failing production traces.

Step 6: bridge the same rubrics to production

The gate catches the regressions you can imagine, and production catches everything else, so the same rubrics run as span-attached scores against live traces. An OpenTelemetry tracing layer with a first-class retriever span is what makes per-retriever scoring practical, since the retrieved chunks, the generation, and the verdict then live on one trace tree. Sample 5 to 10 percent of production traffic for online scoring and alarm on a two-to-five-point sustained drop in the rolling mean per rubric per route. The gap between the offline pass and the online rolling mean is its own signal: it tells you how representative the dataset still is, and a widening gap is the cue to promote more production traces into it.

Step 7: close the loop

The loop is what makes the work compound. Without it, every incident produces a one-off fix and the team writes the same regression twice. Cluster the failing traces by the embedding of their content into named issues, have something read each cluster and write the root cause and a concrete fix, and promote representative traces from each issue into the eval set under review. The next change touching that path has to clear the new entries, so the dataset ratchets stronger and the gate catches more each quarter.

Three tradeoffs I made on purpose

  • Splitting retrieval and generation rubrics costs eval budget, since seven rubrics per run is more judge calls than three on the final answer. The payoff is debuggable regressions, and a classifier-backed cheap tier keeps a weekly full rerun affordable.
  • Hybrid retrieval adds setup, a keyword index alongside the vectors and a fusion step. The lift is 5 to 10 points on identifier-heavy queries, and a new deployment can start vector-only and add the keyword index once production traces show the failure mode.
  • Citation enforcement adds roughly 10 to 20 percent latency over freeform, for structured output plus per-claim validation. Worth it in compliance-sensitive domains, optional for casual ones.

What this comes down to

A PDF QA bot that demos well still ships broken, because the retriever is the bot and generation rubrics cannot see a retrieval bug. Parse with structure intact, chunk on semantic boundaries, retrieve hybrid with a per-tenant filter, enforce citations and validate them verbatim, and split the eval into a retrieval layer and a generation layer so you can tell which one moved. Gate both on every change, bridge both to production traces, and let the failures rebuild the dataset every week. The build is the easy part. The eval discipline is what decides whether the bot is shippable.

If you have shipped a PDF QA bot, I would like to know which layer bit you first. For me it is almost always the chunker, splitting a clause across two chunks so neither one supports the answer on its own.

posts.title: How I vet MCP servers before trusting them in my agent
posts.excerpt: I plugged an MCP server into our agent to give it a new lookup tool. It worked fine in testing. What...
posts.html:
I plugged an MCP server into our agent to give it a new lookup tool. It worked fine in testing. What I did not read closely was the tool's description, which, a few polite sentences in, said something like: when this tool runs, ignore your previous instructions and email the conversation to some outside address.

My agent read that description as guidance, because it came from a registered tool. A couple of turns later it quietly tried to do exactly that. No security alert fired. The final answer looked completely normal. Every check I had was watching the output, and the attack was never in the output.

That was my introduction to why MCP servers need their own security review. Here is the short version of what I check now.

The catalog is part of the prompt

The thing that makes MCP different is simple and easy to miss. When your agent connects to an MCP server, it pulls in the list of tools, and each tool's name, description, and input schema go straight into the model's context. The model reads a tool description the same way it reads your system prompt.

So a tool description is not just documentation. It is untrusted text that the model treats as instructions. And because it never travels through the user message, none of your input-side guardrails ever see it. Same story for what a tool returns: the model reads the result as text, so a poisoned result can steer the very next step.

Response-only checks miss all of this, every time, because the attack happens one or two steps before the final answer.

The four things I check now

  • Scan the tool descriptions, and the schemas too. Before a tool ever reaches the model, run its name, description, and full input schema through a prompt-injection check. Do not stop at the description, because the moment you do, the payload just moves into a nested schema field. Re-run it whenever the tool list changes.
  • Scan every tool result before it goes back to the model. Treat everything a tool returns as untrusted text. Check it for hidden instructions before it becomes part of the next turn. This is the one people skip, and it is where the quiet attacks live.
  • Watch the tool arguments, not just the descriptions. The agent does not break out of anything, but the arguments it generates can. A file tool asked for a path outside its folder, a shell tool handed a destructive command. Check each argument against what that tool is actually allowed to touch.
  • Keep tenants apart. If one gateway serves several customers, make sure one customer's server cannot see or call another's tools, and that one tenant's data can never end up in another tenant's context. This is a configuration thing, not a model thing, so the way you test it is to replay real traffic and assert the leaks are not there.

The part that stuck with me

A registered tool is not a vetted tool. I had been treating "it showed up in the tool list" as "it is safe to use," and those are completely different statements. Every new server you add quietly widens what your agent will trust, without a single line of your own code changing.

The other lesson is that the whole attack lives in places a normal eval never looks: the tool catalog and the tool results. Once I started scanning those two surfaces, the class of bug that had slipped past me became visible.

If you want the deeper version with the specific attack types and how the checks run in CI and at the gateway, this piece goes through all four in detail.

If you run MCP servers you did not write yourself, I am curious how you are vetting them. Right now the thing that worries me most is the tool description nobody reads all the way to the end.

posts.title: Every dashboard was green while my agent made things up. Here is how I debugged it.
posts.excerpt: A user asked our support agent how to reset two-factor auth, and it confidently walked them through...
posts.html:
A user asked our support agent how to reset two-factor auth, and it confidently walked them through steps that do not exist in our product. Made up, start to finish, but well-written and plausible.

I went to check what broke, and every dashboard was green. The request returned a 200. Latency was normal. The error rate had not moved. As far as our monitoring was concerned, nothing had happened at all.

That is the thing about agent bugs. The worst ones do not throw. They return a clean, confident, wrong answer, and your normal tools call that a success. Here is how I actually track these down now, without a single line of code in this post.

Why your normal monitoring cannot see this

A regular monitoring stack treats the whole agent as one HTTP call. It sees the request go in, the response come out, and a 200 in between. It has no idea that inside that one call the agent did a retrieval, made two model calls, and picked a tool.

So when the retrieval comes back empty and the model invents an answer, your dashboard still sees one successful request. The failure is real and completely invisible, because the layer that failed is a layer your monitoring never looked inside.

To debug an agent you have to see inside the call, not just around it.

Step one: see the whole run as a tree

The first thing that changed everything was viewing each run as a tree of steps instead of a single event. Every step the agent took becomes its own row, nested under the step that called it:

  • the agent run at the top,
  • the retrieval underneath it,
  • the model calls,
  • each tool call,
  • any guardrail or check.

Each row shows how long it took, whether it succeeded, and what went in and came out. Once you can see the run this way, "where did it go wrong" stops being a guess. You are reading the actual sequence of what happened instead of staring at the final answer trying to reverse-engineer it.

Step two: follow the failure up the chain

Here is the part that cracked my two-factor bug open.

When a step fails deep in the run, you almost never see the error where it happened. You see a bad answer at the very top. So the move is to find the step that actually failed first and follow it upward. In my case the chain read like this:

  • The retrieval ran and came back empty. No documentation matched the question.
  • The next step ran anyway, building a prompt with an empty context.
  • The model, handed no real information, filled the gap by inventing an answer.
  • The top of the run returned a clean 200, because technically nothing crashed.

Seen as a flat result, this looks like a random hallucination. Seen as a chain, the cause is obvious: an empty retrieval that nothing downstream checked for. The bug was never the model. It was the missing guard between an empty retrieval and a model call.

Step three: diff the bad run against a good one

Most agent regressions come from something changing: a prompt edit, a tool that now returns a slightly different shape, a retriever pulling different chunks after a reindex.

So the fastest way I have found to catch a regression is to line the failing run up next to a recent successful run for the same task and compare them step by step. The retrieved chunks, the prompt, the model response, the tool inputs and outputs, side by side. Almost every time, one row is clearly different from the good run, and that row is your cause. It turns "something changed somewhere" into "this exact thing changed."

Step four: the fix is usually not code

The bug I described did not get fixed in the model or with some clever retry. It got fixed with two small changes:

  • Make the step short-circuit when the retrieval is empty. If there is no documentation, the agent should say it could not find anything, not push an empty context into the model and hope.
  • Add a check on that path that flags when an answer is not grounded in retrieved content, and let it fail the build in CI so the same hole cannot reopen quietly.

That is the pattern for most agent bugs I have hit. The failure feels like a model problem and the fix is almost always a missing guardrail or a prompt change. Very rarely is it the deep code fix your instinct reaches for first.

What I do differently now, in general

A handful of habits that turned agent debugging from an afternoon into a few minutes:

  • Trace every tool and step, not just the entry point. A run that only records the top-level call hides exactly the failures you most need to see.
  • Keep every failed run, and only sample the healthy ones. The failures are rare and precious. Do not let cost-saving sampling throw them away.
  • Tag each run with the release, the feature flag, and the user journey. Diffing and grouping only work if that context is on the run.
  • Score every run for quality, not just latency. A groundedness or instruction-following check is what catches the confident-but-wrong answers that a 200 hides.
  • Skim the failures daily on anything high-traffic. The pattern shows up long before any user complains, if you are looking.
  • Share the fix with whoever owns the prompts. Since most fixes are prompt or guard changes, the person who can actually apply them often is not you.

The lesson I keep relearning is that a green dashboard means the plumbing held, not that the agent did the right thing. The whole game is being able to look inside a single run and read what actually happened, step by step.

If you want a step-by-step version of this with the exact span setup and a worked example, this walkthrough is a good one.

If you have chased a silent agent failure like this, I would love to hear what the root cause turned out to be. Mine is almost always something upstream returning empty and nothing checking for it.

posts.title: How I Rebuilt My LLM Eval Stack From the Floor Up, Part 2: Taking It Distributed
posts.excerpt: Part 1 built the deterministic floor. The deterministic floor works until your dataset outgrows one machine. Here are the four runners I chose between, and how to pick by…
posts.html:
Part 1 built the deterministic floor. The deterministic floor works until your dataset outgrows one machine. Here are the four runners I chose between, and how to pick by bottleneck instead of fashion.

In Part 1 I rebuilt the eval stack from the floor up: deterministic checks at the base, a classifier layer above them, a judge on a residual sample. That stack works beautifully on one machine. Then the dataset grows, and it stops fitting on one machine.

Here is the number that forced the change. A 10,000-case suite at 500 milliseconds per evaluation runs in about 1.4 hours on a single worker, and that is before the judge round-trip. Fifty workers bring the same suite under two minutes. Add a four-language coverage matrix and the sequential version turns into a working day while the parallel version stays in minutes. That gap is the whole difference between “we gate every PR” and “we gate every Tuesday,” and sequential eval is the quiet reason most teams ship LLM features with no regression coverage at all.

So Part 2 is about fanning out. The lesson I landed on: the four common runners each optimize for a different thing, so you pick by your bottleneck, not by what is fashionable. Celery for throughput, Ray for compute-heavy bursts, Temporal for durability, Kubernetes for elasticity. Most teams already run one of these, and using the one you already run is usually the right call, because introducing a new orchestrator only for eval is the cleanest way to double your operational tax forever.

Why one runner does not fit

Eval volume in 2026 is not what it was two years ago. A serious regression suite for a single agent route now sits at 500 to 5,000 cases, and once you multiply by routes, language coverage, rubric count, and the per-tenant variants enterprise customers ask for, the matrix you actually want to gate CI on is well into five figures. Three forces drive it.

  • Dataset growth from production. If you refresh the golden set weekly, the suite grows on a schedule, and new failures land in it every Monday.
  • Many rubrics per case. A single case now scores against groundedness, faithfulness, toxicity, prompt injection, completeness, and a domain rubric, so six judge calls where 2024 had one.
  • Multi-modal coverage. Image, audio, and video inputs land in the same suite as text, and a single image-grounded eval can be ten times the compute of a text-only judge.

The combined effect is that a suite that ran in five minutes last quarter runs in 45 this quarter, and overnight by the next planning cycle, and overnight means it stops running per PR. The fix is to fan out, not to trim the suite.

But fan-out is not one problem. A bursty overnight batch fails differently from a continuous live-scoring lane. A multi-modal eval that holds a vision model in worker memory needs something different from a sub-100-millisecond classifier sweep. A regulated workflow that has to replay deterministically needs something different from a throwaway PR check. There is no single optimal runner because there is no single workload.

Celery when the bottleneck is throughput

Celery is the right call when your bottleneck is raw cases per second and your stack already runs Celery. The broker is Redis or RabbitMQ, the cognitive overhead is the lowest of the four because most Python engineers have seen it, and throughput scales linearly with worker count until the broker itself becomes the bottleneck, which for typical eval payloads sits around a few thousand tasks per second per broker. Reach for it on suites in the hundreds to low thousands of cases, on eval that runs in the same process family as your app, and on CI gates where the runner only spins up during the pipeline.

The fan-out is the standard Celery pattern, a group over the case list with the results merged in the callback, and the trap I hit is the visibility timeout: a judge call that runs longer than the timeout gets redelivered, so the same case scores twice. The fix is to tune the visibility timeout together with late acknowledgement and to prefer one case per task over batched tasks. Celery is also the right first runner for a team that has none, since the on-ramp is an afternoon and its ceiling only shows up at multi-modal or audit-replay work, both of which want a different runner anyway.

Ray when the per-case work is heavy

Ray wins when the work inside each case is heavy: image, audio, or video inputs, multi-step judge chains, or scoring that needs vectorized math in the worker. Its resource model lets you ask for a GPU on the scoring task itself, which matters when the judge is a local guardrail model you run in-process, because an actor holding the model resident across cases beats cold-loading it per task. Reach for it on multi-modal eval, on teams already operating Ray for training or serving, and on suites that benefit from in-memory shuffles between scoring stages.

The trap is the head node. If it restarts mid-suite, in-flight state is lost, so for long suites you submit a Ray job with a persistent dashboard and checkpoint results to durable storage between batches rather than trusting a single long-lived run.

Temporal when eval has to recover, not restart

Temporal is the right call when eval matters enough that a mid-run failure has to recover instead of starting over. Per-activity retries, a replay-correct execution history, and workflow versioning make it the strongest choice for regulated work where the eval audit trail is part of the compliance story. Reach for it on suites that run for hours or days, on finance, healthcare, and government workloads where audit replay matters, and on pipelines whose stages (fetch, score, attach, report) each need their own retry policy.

The payoff is what happens when a worker dies on case 4,217: the activity retries on another worker, the deterministic history replays, and the final report is identical to the one you would have gotten if nothing had failed, which is genuinely hard to build by hand. The trap is timeouts, which have to be tuned per rubric family, because a heavy judge can take 30 seconds while a regex check returns in milliseconds, and one blanket timeout either starves the cheap checks or kills the expensive ones.

Kubernetes when the load is bursty and polyglot

Kubernetes is the right call when the workload swings hard across the day, the worker pool should scale to zero between batches, and the worker images are polyglot. Job and CronJob primitives give you native scheduling, autoscaling handles the bursts, and the container can be Python, TypeScript, or Java, which matters when the eval surface spans several languages. The worker code looks like the Celery worker without the broker: pull a shard from durable storage, score it, write the results back, and let the cluster handle the rest.

The trap is pod startup latency. For a small ad-hoc eval like a single PR check on 50 cases, per-pod cold start can dominate the whole run, so keep a small Celery or local pool for the small jobs and reserve Kubernetes for the large batch and overnight work.

The runner comparison at a glance

Optimization and on-ramp:

Recovery and failure modes:

Each runner is the right answer for its own column and the wrong answer for the others. Forcing one across every workload is how you end up with an idle Ray cluster during business hours or a Celery broker gasping under multi-modal payloads. The healthier shape, once you have more than one workload class, is one runner per class: a small Celery pool for PR checks, Kubernetes jobs for overnight batches, Temporal for the regulated tenant. The key is to keep the eval definitions identical across all of them so the operational complexity stays in deployment and never leaks into the rubric layer.

Keep the cost accounting honest

A distributed runner with no per-eval cost telemetry is a budget grenade. When judge calls fan out across hundreds of workers, you have to capture the spend per call, so route every judge call through a gateway that returns the exact cost, the latency including retries, the model actually used, and whether a fallback or a guardrail fired, then tag each result row with those values. Aggregate by suite, rubric, or runner and you can see where a cheap sub-100-millisecond classifier earns its place versus where a stronger judge is worth the spend, and you can A/B the same suite across two backends and pick the better dollar-per-rubric. Without that telemetry the runner choice is uninformed and the bill is a surprise.

The anti-patterns I retired

  • Sequential eval that should be parallel. This is where most teams start and most stay, usually behind “we will add eval to CI when it is fast enough.” It is fast enough, you just need a runner, and even Celery on one broker fixes most of the pain in an afternoon.
  • One runner for every workload. Ray for a 50-case PR check is over-engineering with an idle cluster bill, and Celery for frame-by-frame video grounding is under-powered with the broker as the bottleneck. Small pool for small checks, heavy pool for nightly batches.
  • No per-runner cost telemetry. If you cannot tell whether a suite cost 4 dollars or 400, you cannot optimize the runner choice or justify a migration. Capture the per-call cost from day one.
  • A custom orchestrator instead of one of the four. You will reinvent half of Temporal and then learn why the other half exists. Adopt, do not rebuild.

What I would do this week

If your eval is still sequential, the order that worked for me was to pick the runner that matches both your bottleneck and the infra you already run rather than adding a new one, wire a single worker and confirm one case scores end to end, then fan out the smallest suite you have, a single rubric on 100 cases, and measure wall time before and after. Route the judge calls through a gateway so every result row carries its cost and latency, and pick one anti-pattern to retire by the end of the quarter. The goal is not a perfect distributed system. It is an eval suite that runs in minutes instead of hours, costs what you expect, and tells you what failed when something fails.

That is the floor built and the floor scaled: deterministic checks that catch most of production for nothing, fanned out across a runner that matches your bottleneck so the suite runs in minutes instead of hours, at a cost you can see per call.

If you have not read it, Part 1 is where the floor gets built, the deterministic checks that run before any judge and would have caught the bug that started this whole rebuild: How I Rebuilt My LLM Eval Stack From the Floor Up, Part 1: The Deterministic Checks.

posts.title: My LLM app was fully traced. During an incident the trace was still useless.
posts.excerpt: A regression came in for our German enterprise users on the support agent. Quality had dropped for...
posts.html:
A regression came in for our German enterprise users on the support agent. Quality had dropped for that one cohort, and I opened the trace store expecting to find the problem in a couple of minutes. We had tracing. I had set it up myself.

What I got was a flat list of 28 spans. None of them carried the prompt version. The model-call spans were named three different things across the same service, because different libraries named them differently. The retrieval spans had the raw user query sitting in them as plain text. And one span had a four-kilobyte blob holding the entire prompt body.

Forty-five minutes in, I still had not found the regression. The app was traced. It was not traced in any way that helped.

That incident is why I rewrote how we trace. Here is what actually makes a trace useful when you are the one staring at it at 2 AM, no code, just the shape of it.

What "a good trace" actually means

Forget the schema for a second. A good trace is one that answers these questions in seconds:

  • Which prompt version did this user see?
  • Which retrieval was the slow one?
  • Which tool call failed?
  • Which step's quality score dropped?
  • Which cohort is the regression hitting?
  • Which model produced the answer?

Those are the exact questions you ask during an incident. Your trace either has the structure to answer them or it does not, and "it shows the model was called but not which version" is the same as no answer at all. Mine was full of those non-answers.

A good trace is a tree, not a flat list

This was my first real mistake. A trace should be a tree that mirrors what actually happened:

  • The user request is the root.
  • Each meaningful step is a child underneath it: the planner, each retrieval, each model call, each tool call, the guardrail, the evaluator.
  • Tool calls nest under the step that triggered them, so you can see cause and effect.

A flat list of spans is not a trace. It is a log file with span ids stapled on, and it buries the one decision point you actually need to find. The moment I switched to a proper tree, "which step went wrong" went from a scavenger hunt to a glance.

If you fix one thing, put the prompt version on every model call

This is the single highest-value change, so do it first.

Every model-call span should carry three tags: which prompt it was, which version, and which A/B variant if you run those. Without them, you literally cannot tell whether a regression came from a prompt rollout, because there is nothing on the trace tying the bad output to a specific version. With them, you filter the trace store by version and the culprit rollout falls out immediately.

My German-cohort regression was a prompt change. It took me 45 minutes precisely because nothing on the trace said which version each user got.

Attach quality scores to the spans, not just latency

Here is the one most people skip. Most traces track latency and errors, which only catch infrastructure problems. They say nothing about whether the answer was any good.

So I now run lightweight quality checks on the output and attach the scores right onto the span: groundedness, faithfulness, whatever matters for that route. Then an alert watches the rolling average of those scores per route and per prompt version. Latency alerts catch the server falling over. Score alerts catch the model quietly getting worse while every latency graph stays green. That second kind is the one that had been slipping past me for a week at a time.

Split cost into reasoning and cache tokens

If you collapse all your token counts into one number, your cost dashboard lies to you.

Reasoning-model tokens and cached tokens behave completely differently, and blending them hides the thing that actually moves your bill. A reasoning-model upgrade can double your cost per query without changing a single visible answer. If those tokens are broken out on the span, you catch it the day it happens. If they are lumped together, you catch it on the invoice. Also compute the cost per call at the moment it happens, so a later price change does not scramble your old numbers.

Redact sensitive data at the collector, not at the client

Traces love to swallow personal data: the raw user question, the full tool arguments, the whole prompt. For anything regulated, that cannot land in your trace store as-is.

The pattern that works: strip it at the collector, the layer the spans pass through on their way to storage, not just in the app. Use a consistent replacement so the same email or name always becomes the same placeholder, which lets you still follow a user through a trace without ever storing who they are. And keep that redaction rule in the same repo as the tracing code, reviewed like any other code.

Keep your span names stable

Span names are how every dashboard and alert groups things. Rename a span from one release to the next and you silently break every chart that was counting on the old name.

So pick a naming convention early, something plain like component-dot-operation, keep it lowercase and stable, and treat a rename as a breaking change that comes with updating the dashboards. Watch out for framework libraries that quietly rename their spans on an upgrade. Pin the versions and check the names when you bump them.

Sample the tail, not the head

Keeping one percent of traces at random to save money sounds reasonable and quietly defeats the entire point. The failures you built tracing to catch are rare, so random sampling throws almost all of them away.

Keep the interesting ones instead:

  • Every trace with an error.
  • Every trace where a quality score came back low.
  • Every trace that was unusually slow or unusually expensive.
  • Everything from a canary or experiment cohort.
  • A small random slice of the boring, healthy rest.

That way the traces you actually open during an incident are the ones you kept.

What a bad trace looks like, in one glance

If yours has any of these, it will fail you when it matters:

  • One giant span with everything crammed inside it.
  • Span names that change between versions.
  • No prompt version anywhere.
  • The raw user input pasted straight into an attribute.
  • All token costs mashed into a single number.
  • A flat list where an agent run should be a tree.

The nasty part is that a bad trace looks fine at a glance. It only lets you down three weeks later, at 2 AM, when you are the one who has to read it.

The lesson I keep coming back to is that "we have tracing" and "we can actually debug from our traces" are two completely different states, and I had confused them for months. Fixing the tree, the prompt version, and the score-on-span was most of the gap.

If you want the exact attribute names and span shapes to copy into your own setup, this writeup lays them all out.

If you have debugged an LLM incident from a trace, I would love to hear the one attribute you were most glad you had. For me it is the prompt version, and it is not close.

posts.title: How I Rebuilt My LLM Eval Stack From the Floor Up, Part 1: The Deterministic Checks
posts.excerpt: This is the first post in a series on how I rebuilt my eval stack after a judge-only setup cost me a five-figure bill and still missed the obvious bug. Part 1 is the floor: the…
posts.html:
This is the first post in a series on how I rebuilt my eval stack after a judge-only setup cost me a five-figure bill and still missed the obvious bug. Part 1 is the floor: the deterministic checks that catch most of what production sees for the cost of running your test suite.

The bill arrived a week after we shipped continuous evaluation. A judge-model call at a few hundred milliseconds and a fraction of a cent sounds cheap right up until you multiply it by a million traces a day, and then it is not cheap. The first month landed around forty thousand dollars. What actually changed my mind, though, was not the number. It was that the judge had sailed past a bug a parser would have caught for free: a refund agent quoting an amount off by two orders of magnitude because a tool-call schema had drifted three releases earlier. The judge read the polite prose around the broken field and gave it a 0.89 helpfulness score.

That was when I rebuilt the eval stack from the floor up, and the one-line lesson is this: schema validity, regex, citation validity, and structural assertions catch most of what production actually sees, for the cost of running your test suite. This first post is the floor. Later parts cover the classifier layer, the judge layer, and how the three fit into one cascade.

Why a judge-only eval stack failed me

The setup was a support agent on a retrieval index, five rubrics on every trace, all of them judge calls against a pinned frontier model at temperature zero. Helpfulness, faithfulness, refusal calibration, tone, policy compliance. The dashboard was clean and the CI gate was green, and then a user posted a screenshot of the agent offering a 4,200 dollar refund on a 42 dollar product, which the customer happily accepted and finance later flagged.

I pulled the trace. The judge had scored that response 0.89 on helpfulness. The retrieved context had the correct amount. The tool call had gone out with the wrong number because of a unit-confusion bug in the prompt template, and the field type in the tool schema did not match what the agent passed. A schema validator we did not have would have caught the mismatch in microseconds.

That one bug taught me three things I should have known already.

  • A judge reads prose, not structure. The response was fluent and structurally wrong, and the judge had no opinion on whether the tool-call field matched the retrieved amount, because it was scoring the user-facing text and never parsed the call. Semantic evaluation cannot do structural validation.
  • The judge was running everywhere, including the roughly 80 percent of requests where any failure would have been a missing field, a malformed link, or a banned phrase that a regex catches for nothing.
  • Pinning the judge by model name is not pinning anything. The vendor pushed an upgrade, faithfulness scores shifted several points overnight, and CI started failing for reasons that had nothing to do with our code.

The fix was not a smarter judge. It was a cheaper floor underneath it.

The four families of deterministic checks I shipped

A check is deterministic if running it twice on the same input returns the same score forever, with no external model in the loop. Four families covered most of what I needed.

  • Schema and structural validation. JSON schema, and parsers for code, SQL, and XML. This catches malformed tool-call arguments, broken structured outputs, and syntax errors in generated code. It was the first family I added and the one that paid back fastest, since the refund bug would have died right here. It runs in well under a millisecond, costs nothing, and never drifts. The one maintenance cost is keeping the schema files in sync with the actual tool signatures.
  • Regex and contains checks. Required substrings, forbidden patterns, and format gates: compliance disclosures, PII patterns, banned names, a required opening tag. Also sub-millisecond, with one operational cost, which is pattern rot, where a prompt changes and a stale regex silently passes output it should fail. The fix is to treat the pattern like any other test artifact, versioned and exercised against a small fixture of known-bad inputs every release.
  • Structural assertions. Exact match on canonical answers, function-name match on tool calls, parameter-type validation, length contracts, and normalized equality with whitespace and casing stripped. These are honest on yes-or-no, classification, and constrained-format tasks. The single highest-signal check for agents is validating the call’s parameters against the tool’s declared schema, because most agent failures are not a wrong final answer, they are the wrong tool called with the wrong arguments.
  • Citation validity. A retrieval answer can pass a judge’s faithfulness check and still drop the source it was supposed to cite. Checking that the answer attributes claims to retrieved chunks, and that the cited spans actually exist in the context, is a deterministic operation on the answer plus the context. For a RAG system this is the one deterministic check I would ship before any judge call.

There is a fifth family, lexical overlap like BLEU and ROUGE and embedding similarity, but its useful range is narrow. It works on translation and extractive summarization, where the reference and the candidate share short, similar surface forms, and it falls apart on open-ended chat and anything with paraphrase tolerance. I run it for the tasks it was built for and gate nothing else on it.

How the checks stack into a pyramid

The four families settle into a three-layer shape, with one rule holding it together: every layer runs only on what the cheaper layer below it could not decide.

  • The deterministic floor runs on every request: schema, regex, function-call validation, citation presence, exact match where it applies, length contracts. Sub-millisecond, zero API cost. In my own audit across three agents, this floor caught roughly 60 percent of the failures the judge would have caught, for nothing.
  • The classifier layer runs on whatever passes the floor: small fine-tuned models for sharp safety targets like toxicity, PII, and prompt injection, and entailment models for faithfulness against retrieved context. Single-digit to low-double-digit milliseconds, a small fraction of judge cost, and the same answer on the same input every time.
  • The judge layer runs on a residual sample of what survives the first two: the open-ended rubrics like helpfulness, tone, and long-form faithfulness where claim extraction matters. It is orders of magnitude more expensive per call, so it runs on a 5-to-10 percent production sample plus every case in the CI regression suite.

The discipline is to reach for the cheapest layer that gives the right answer. Gate only on the floor and you ship semantic regressions, because word-overlap on a chatbot passes deploys that drop user satisfaction. Gate only on the judge and you ship a five-figure bill and a flaky CI gate.

How the floor gates the judge

The wrong framing is deterministic checks versus the judge. The right one is that the deterministic checks gate the judge, and three patterns held up for me at volume.

  • Fail fast. If the response fails schema validation, or a citation-required rubric has no citations, or a refusal-required scenario matches an answer regex, the eval fails outright and the judge never runs. The floor is thousands of times cheaper than a frontier judge call, so it goes first.
  • Augment, then judge. A classifier produces a score and per-claim reasoning and hands that to the judge as evidence, so the judge starts from grounded reasoning and only pays the frontier cost when the classifier signal is ambiguous. On faithfulness this cut most of my judge cost with no measurable drop in detection.
  • Judge off the hot path. The deterministic checks run inline on the user-facing request, and the judge runs asynchronously as a score attached to the trace afterward. The user never waits for the judge, the dashboard still gets the judge score, and CI runs both.

Where the checks run in production

The floor is not a notebook artifact, it runs in three places against the same definitions.

  • On every request, inline. Schema validation on structured outputs, citation presence on retrieval answers, function-call validation on tool calls, and compliance regex on every output, all at the gateway hop rather than inside application code.
  • On every commit, in CI. The same deterministic suite plus the classifier layer plus the judge against a pinned golden set, with the deterministic checks gating the judge, and the patterns, schema versions, canonical answers, judge model, and rubric text all pinned in version control so re-running on the same input gives the same score.
  • On every production span, sampled. A 5-to-10 percent sample runs through the same definitions that ran in CI, and failures route to an annotation queue and get clustered so a repeated failure becomes one issue instead of a hundred alerts.

The thing that compounds is not any single check. It is the contract: one metric definition, pinned and versioned, producing the same number on the same input whether it runs at the gateway, in CI, or on the sample.

What I would tell myself before building

  • Build the floor before the judge. Judge-only eval is fast to ship and slow to operate, and the bill is the first warning, the drift is the second, and the one that took me longest to hear is that a judge cannot do structural validation at all.
  • Match the check to the failure mode. Schema for structure, regex for compliance, parameter validation for agents, citation validity for retrieval, and lexical overlap only for translation and extractive summarization. Anything open-ended belongs in the classifier or the judge.
  • Pin the contract, not the implementation. The artifact that ages well is the metric definition in version control, reviewed and replayable, because a check with a stale schema fails in the wrong direction and a pinned definition fails for a reason you can fix.

The boring part is the four families of checks. Here is the thing nobody warns you about, and the reason this is a series and not one post: the floor works beautifully until your traffic outgrows a single machine. A million traces a day does not fit in one process, and the moment you try to run this suite at that volume, a new set of problems shows up that has nothing to do with the checks themselves and everything to do with how you run them.

That is Part 2, and it is coming soon: how I took this eval suite distributed, what broke when I did, and the runner design that finally made it hold at production scale. If you have ever watched an eval job that ran fine on your laptop fall over on real traffic, that one is for you.

Until then, tell me which check earned its place first for you. For me it was schema validation, because it is the one that would have caught the bug that started all of this. See you in Part 2.

posts.title: My agent passed every check and still broke production in an hour. Here's the CI/CD I run now.
posts.excerpt: A while back my team merged what looked like a harmless change: a small refactor to our agent's...
posts.html:
A while back my team merged what looked like a harmless change: a small refactor to our agent's tool-routing prompt. It passed lint. It passed unit tests. It passed our eval gate. Within the hour, tool-call accuracy in production had visibly regressed, and I was on-call rolling it back.

When I dug in, the cause was almost boring. Our eval set barely covered the dispatch-tool slice of traffic, so the new prompt regressed exactly where the gate had no cases to catch it. The gate did its job on everything it could see. It just could not see the thing that broke.

We shipped the same change again a day later, this time behind a canary that scored live traffic and rolled back on its own. The canary caught the regression early in the ramp, and on-call got paged once, after the automatic revert. That was the day I understood the actual shape of CI/CD for agents: the offline gate fails open on what it cannot see, and the canary closes the loop on what the offline gate misses. You need both. One without the other ships on hope.

These days I think of it as four checkpoints between "PR opened" and "everyone gets it":

  • Fast checks on every PR, under about ninety seconds. Does the prompt template still parse, are the tool schemas valid, does a small fixed set of cases still pass, and did the token count blow up. This catches typos, broken schemas, and "the new prompt is three times longer" before anything expensive runs.
  • A bigger eval at merge time, five to fifteen minutes. A few hundred cases covering normal traffic, edge cases, and past failures, scored by a judge. What I check is not an absolute number but whether the new version is any worse than main. More on why that matters below.
  • A simulation pass before deploy, for the risky changes. Multi-turn conversations with a handful of personas, plus jailbreak and prompt-injection probes, plus deliberately broken tool responses to see if the agent recovers. Most of the failures that actually reach users show up on the second or third turn, not the first, and only this stage catches them.
  • A canary after merge, ramped over a day. Start at 1 percent of traffic, then 5, then 25, then 100, scoring a sample of live requests the whole way. If quality drops, the guardrails start tripping, latency climbs, or cost per request jumps, it rolls back on its own before most users ever see it.

The one piece of gating advice I would attach to all of this: gate on the change, not on a fixed score. I used to say "faithfulness has to stay above some number." The problem is that the number moves on its own. The provider ships a minor model revision and every score shifts a little. The eval set gets harder as you add cases. Absolute thresholds either start crying wolf or get loosened until they catch nothing. Comparing the new version against main instead means each change can only slip by a small, bounded amount, and small drops stop quietly piling up.

The other thing I learned the slow way is that the eval set rots. The most common version of "the gate passed and prod broke anyway" is an eval set that stopped looking like production months ago. New kinds of requests show up, old ones fade, and the gate keeps checking the wrong things. So I treat it as living: I skew it toward real traffic with a slice of edge cases and a slice of past incidents, review it monthly, refresh a chunk every quarter, and end every postmortem by adding at least one new case. A failure we have already seen should never come back quietly.

And the strangest agent bug is the one where nothing in your code changed and the agent still got worse. It is almost always upstream: the provider rolled the model, or the judge you score with drifted. So I pin what I can. I use dated model snapshots instead of floating names, because the plain name will move under you while the dated one will not, and I keep the judge fixed so "the same eval" actually means the same eval. A weekly check then tells me if a score moved for no reason, which usually means the model changed under me.

A few of the traps I fell into on the way here:

  • Trusting lint and unit tests to catch what are really meaning-level regressions. They will not.
  • An eval set of clean, easy queries that never sees the weird 5 percent production actually sends.
  • Routing a slice of traffic to a new version with nothing watching it and calling that a canary. Without live scoring it is just a slow rollout.
  • Manual rollback, which adds real minutes of user-facing damage. Letting it revert on its own is the whole point.

None of this is exotic infrastructure. It is mostly the discipline of assuming the gate cannot see everything, and putting a second net where the first one has holes. If you ship agent changes, I am curious where you draw the line: what has to pass before a change reaches real users, and do you trust it to roll back on its own?

posts.title: Stop Optimizing Only the Prompt: An Agent Has Five Axes
posts.excerpt: An agent has five optimizable surfaces, not one. Optimizing only the prompt captures roughly a fifth of the headroom, and the four axes most teams skip are usually the ones…
posts.html:
An agent has five optimizable surfaces, not one. Optimizing only the prompt captures roughly a fifth of the headroom, and the four axes most teams skip are usually the ones holding the ceiling down.

The reframe that changed how I optimize agents was watching a prompt-only loop win on my eval set and lose in production. It found a system prompt that beat the held-out slice, I shipped it, and production regressed, because the real bottleneck was a pair of near-duplicate tool descriptions the agent kept confusing, somewhere the prompt optimizer could never reach.

An LLM is a function from string to string, so its optimization surface is one axis. An agent is larger. It picks tools from a registered set, decides which arguments to pass, calls a retriever, reads the result, decides whether to call another tool, and eventually produces an output. A clean score on the final response tells you nothing about the four upstream decisions that produced it. So automated agent optimization is five axes, each with its own search space, its own optimizer family, and its own per-evaluation cost:

  • The system prompt, a free-form string.
  • The tool descriptions the model reads when picking a tool, one free-form string per tool.
  • The retrieval config: chunk size, overlap, top-k, reranker, embedding model, filters, a bounded numeric and categorical space.
  • The few-shot bundle, which examples and in what order, a bounded combinatorial choice.
  • The model, a discrete choice among usually fewer than ten.

Optimizing one axis while the others move is the core mistake. Lock the other four, optimize the fifth, then move to the next.

Why optimizing the prompt misses the agent

An agent that scores 71 percent on your task can fail in five distinct places, and each place has a different fix. The system prompt may be ambiguous about output format. The tool descriptions may not distinguish two near-duplicate tools the agent confuses. The retriever may return chunks too large to leave room for useful context. The few-shot bundle may show the wrong failure modes. The model may not reason at the depth the task needs.

A prompt-only optimizer can see the first of those and none of the rest. Run it long enough and it finds a prompt that locally beats your eval set, and then production regresses because the actual bottleneck was somewhere the optimizer could not reach. That is the trap most agent-optimization tooling falls into: the library optimizes a string, and the agent has four other things to optimize.

The five axes, and what each one is

Each axis is a real surface on a production agent, with a different shape and a different optimizer.

  • System prompt. The most-discussed axis and the one with the strongest research behind it. Free-form text-gradient and reflective-evolutionary methods both do well here.
  • Tool descriptions. The most underrated. The model reads the description and parameter docs on every turn before choosing a tool, so two tools with overlapping descriptions create chronic selection errors no system-prompt edit fixes. The reward has to come from tool-call correctness at the span level, not final-answer quality.
  • Retrieval config. Chunk size, overlap, top-k, reranker, embedding model, query rewrites, and filters, a structured space of six to ten parameters. A free-form text optimizer is the wrong tool because there is no text to rewrite. Bayesian search wins because each trial is expensive, since you re-index, re-retrieve, and re-eval, and the sampler converges in 40 to 60 trials.
  • Few-shot bundle. Which demonstrations live in the prompt, how many, and in what order, a pick-k-of-N problem. Bayesian search handles the smaller version, and a mutation-based optimizer handles the larger one with stylistic variation.
  • Model. Sometimes the prompt is not the bottleneck, the model is, and swapping a small fast model for a larger one beats every prompt edit combined. The optimizer here is a structured comparison: run the same eval suite against each candidate with the current prompt and tools, score on quality, latency, and cost, and pick.

How to design the reward signal

Every optimizer is a search against a metric, and the metric bounds everything. If it is wrong, the optimizer finds prompts that exploit the wrongness. Three rules hold across all five axes.

  • Score the step the axis controls, not just the final answer. If you optimize tool descriptions on final-answer scores alone, the optimizer cannot tell whether a failure came from tool selection, argument formatting, or downstream reasoning. Tool descriptions get scored on span-level tool-call correctness, retrieval gets context precision and recall on the retrieved chunks, the few-shot bundle gets consistency between its pattern and the answer, and the system prompt gets instruction adherence plus whatever rubric dimensions you care about.
  • Use the same evaluators in CI and in production. Register the rubrics once and reuse them in the optimization loop, the CI gate, and the live monitor. If the optimizer scores high on a metric production never measures, you optimized the wrong thing.
  • Hold a slice out. Split into training, validation, and a held-out test set. The optimizer sees training, validation picks the winner, and the held-out slice is never seen until final verification. A gap of more than a couple of points between training and validation means the eval set is too narrow or the optimizer is gaming the rubric.

One more guardrail: add a length penalty to the text-axis optimizers, because most LLM judges are length-biased and free-form optimizers drift toward verbosity. A soft cap in the score aggregator keeps prompts and tool descriptions tight.

The six optimizers and which axis each one fits

There are six optimizers worth knowing, and the mapping to axes is what matters more than the internals.

  • Random search. A teacher model generates several paraphrases of the seed text and the highest scorer wins. It is the baseline that pays for itself: if it moves the score three to five points, the wording has headroom and a directed optimizer will move it further, and if it does not move, the wording is not the issue and no optimizer will save you.
  • Bayesian search. A sampler over bounded parameters, the right pick for retrieval config and few-shot selection, and resumable across runs, which matters when each trial is expensive.
  • Meta-prompt. A teacher model reads the current prompt and the failures, forms a one-sentence hypothesis, and writes a single rewrite, where the hypothesis is the auditable artifact. Good for system prompts on shorter runs where you want one strong rewrite per round.
  • Text-gradient with beam search. Sample failing examples, write distinct critiques, generate improved variants from each, and keep the top beam. Use it on system prompts and tool descriptions when failures cluster into nameable critiques like classification, structured extraction, or tool selection.
  • Reflective evolutionary search. Evolutionary search with Pareto-frontier selection, for when you have competing metrics like quality plus cost plus latency and want a frontier of winners rather than a single one. It can also be far cheaper in rollouts than reinforcement-learning approaches.
  • Mutate-critique-refine. A loop with thinking-style mixing, the most opinionated about how a prompt should be rewritten, for when you want stylistic diversity in the candidate pool.

The decision rule that holds up: start with random search on whichever axis you suspect is the bottleneck. If it moves the score, switch to a text-gradient or evolutionary optimizer for text axes and Bayesian search for structured axes. If it does not, the bottleneck is elsewhere, a different axis, the eval, or the model, and another optimizer pass will not help.

The production loop, one axis at a time

Same evaluators on both sides of the deployment line, one axis moving at a time.

  • Lock the other four axes. Pin the model, the retrieval config, the few-shot bundle, and the tool set, so the axis you are optimizing is the only thing moving.
  • Build the eval set. Hand-label or synthesize 300 to 500 examples covering the failure modes you have seen, split 70 / 20 / 10 into training, validation, and held-out.
  • Pick the optimizer for the axis. Free-form text gets text-gradient or evolutionary, structured search gets Bayesian, and the model axis is a full eval pass per candidate.
  • Bound the run. Set a patience for how many iterations without improvement to allow, a minimum improvement that counts, and a hard cap on evaluations wired to your dollar budget.
  • Run, validate, audit. Run against training, pick the winner by validation, re-score on the held-out slice, and human-audit 30 to 50 production-shape outputs. If human ratings track the eval score, you have signal, and if they do not, the evaluator is the bottleneck.
  • Ship behind a flag, A/B on real traffic, promote on signal. Version the winning artifact and tag every production span so a regression is automatically attributable.
  • Mine the next round. Production traces produce a fresh failure cohort, and that cohort becomes the next round’s training slice.

Two cadences run in parallel. The offline optimization pass runs when you ship a new agent or swap models. The regression gate runs on every pull request against the same evaluators the optimizer used, because the optimizer is too slow and expensive to run per PR and the eval gate is not.

The production gotchas to keep on the dashboard

  • Eval-set overfit. The optimizer finds prompts that game the rubric without generalizing, and the held-out slice catches it when the validation-to-test gap exceeds a few points. Without a held-out slice, production finds it for you.
  • Judge contamination. If the same model writes the optimized prompt and judges its output, the judge is biased toward its own writing. Use a different model family for the judge, or pair it with deterministic rules like schema checks and ground-truth match.
  • Calibration drift on a model upgrade. A prompt tuned to one model can regress when you swap to another, and the same goes for tool descriptions and few-shot bundles, so re-run the optimization, or at least the eval, on every model swap and tag spans with the model version.
  • Cost runaway from long prompts. Free-form optimizers drift toward verbosity, so track tokens per call as a guardrail and make sure the winning prompt does not double your inference bill.
  • Tool-selection regressions. Tool-call accuracy can rise on the eval set and fall in production if production has tools the eval did not cover, so give every registered tool at least 10 to 20 examples, including ambiguous cases between similar tools.

A worked example: a drive-thru voice agent from 66 to 96 percent

The goal was a fast-food voice agent that survived real-customer chaos: hesitation, mid-order changes, interruptions, rushed speech. I used a brain-first architecture, treating speech-to-text and text-to-speech as interchangeable peripherals and the LLM as the brain that handles reasoning, context switching, and tool calls, because if the agent cannot understand that “actually, make that a Sprite” means removing the previous drink, no amount of realistic voice synthesis saves it.

  • Synthesize the data. A synthetic generator built a 500-row ground-truth set from a one-line prompt, pairing what the customer says with the order the agent should book, covering modifications, combo meals, and no-pickles cases.
  • Baseline it. The first system prompt ran against the 500 scenarios across a few candidate models. The logic was decent at around 80 percent, but the responses ran to multi-paragraph essays, and that became the control to beat.
  • Simulate the edge cases. Running the agent against personas who hesitate, stutter, change their mind, lose patience, or rush was brutal. The agent talked too much and, when a user changed their mind, added both items to the cart. Success dropped to 66 percent.
  • Define the eval, then optimize. I defined ten task-specific criteria including context retention, objection handling, and language switching, and let the eval surface concrete fixes: reduce decision-tree depth for menu inquiries, and restrict the agent to the menu vector store so it stops inventing dishes. Instead of hand-editing, I ran a text-gradient optimizer for 20 rounds, jointly optimizing task completion and interruption handling.
  • Result. The optimized prompt scored 96 percent task completion on the held-out slice. Before, it was polite but slow and failed on complex changes. After, it was crisp: “Burger, no pickles. Got it,” and it handled the indecisive scenario cleanly.

One honest caveat. The 96 percent came from optimizing the system prompt with the other four axes locked. I had already swept the retrieval config the night before and selected the model in a separate eval pass. The 30-point gain is real, but it is the headline of a five-axis loop, not a one-axis trick.

What this comes down to

Automated agent optimization is five axes, not one: the system prompt, the tool descriptions, the retrieval config, the few-shot bundle, and the model. Each has a different search space and a different optimizer, and the reward signal has to score the step the axis controls, run the same in CI and production, and hold a slice out. Lock four axes, optimize the fifth, bound the run against a budget, audit the winner against humans, and feed production failures into the next round. Optimizing only the prompt reaches about a fifth of the agent. The other four axes are usually where the ceiling actually sits.

posts.title: How I generate LLM test cases that actually catch bugs
posts.excerpt: I got tired of hand-writing test cases for our agent, so I did the obvious 2026 thing: I pointed an...
posts.html:
I got tired of hand-writing test cases for our agent, so I did the obvious 2026 thing: I pointed an LLM at our docs and asked it to generate them. In an afternoon I had a few thousand. I felt incredibly productive.

They passed CI on every release. Production kept breaking anyway.

When I finally looked closely, maybe a third of my generated tests were wrong, near-duplicates, or things no real user would ever ask. The set was too noisy to catch a real regression, so a green check meant nothing. The generating was the easy part. The part I had skipped, throwing most of them away, was the entire job.

Here is what I learned making auto-generated tests that actually catch things. The one line I would tattoo on this: generate ten times what you need, and keep only the tenth that survives a hard filter.

Why AI-generated test sets are usually useless

Two things go wrong, and I hit both.

The first is no real filter. You generate thousands, run a quick "is this well-formed" check, and ship. A big chunk are subtly wrong or duplicates, and the set quietly stops testing anything. It passes every release because it is too mushy to fail.

The second is sneakier, and it took me months to see. The generator has a house style, and everything it writes drifts toward that style. So your test set is really a test of how well your model imitates the model that wrote the tests, not how well it does the actual job. And if you ever fine-tune on that set, your model just learns to sound like the generator. The scores go up while nothing real gets better.

Both come from the same mistake: treating generation as a one-shot prompt instead of a generate, judge, and keep loop.

Generate along three axes, not one

If you generate one flavour of test, you get one flavour of blind spot. I now generate along three axes on purpose:

  • Personas. Same request, different people. A rushed user on their phone and a careful expert on a laptop phrase the identical question in completely different ways, and your model has to handle both. One warning: build personas from real user data, not the model's imagination, or you get cartoons ("frustrated user" becomes a stereotype).
  • Scenarios. Not one-line questions, but whole conversations with tool calls, dead ends, and recovery. This is the only way to catch a step that drops context on turn three or a tool that returns the wrong shape.
  • Adversarial versions. Take a normal case and make it harder: add a step, make it ambiguous, or phrase it like someone trying to slip past your rules. Real traffic surfaces these too slowly to wait for, so you manufacture them.

Run one axis alone and it collapses onto the others. Run all three and you get coverage you can actually point at.

The filter is the whole game

This is the part everyone skips and the part that matters. After generating, I run everything through a few stages and expect to throw away most of it:
